meta.regime: The war premium is being dismantled by diplomacy rather than by data: Trump said on Sunday that restarting the war on Iran is highly unlikely if talks progress, and oil fell again through a weekend in which the IRGC said it hit three more tankers and Washington widened its blockade. That splits the board cleanly - the Fed's hawkish case is domestic and survives into a December 9 vote it takes without ever seeing the energy collapse in a CPI print, while the ECB, BoE, RBA, RBNZ and Bank of Canada all built theirs on an imported input that is now deflating on a political timetable, and the franc loses the only leg it had.
meta.nextBigEvent: US October CPI, Tuesday November 10 at 13:30Z, forecast plus 0.3% m/m headline against plus 0.6% previous and plus 0.2% core against plus 0.3%. It is the last inflation print the Fed sees before December 9, because November's report does not arrive until December 10, the day after the vote, and because it covers October it predates the entire energy collapse. CME FedWatch is now around 78% to 80% for a December hike against 76.8% on November 6 and roughly 70% before the payrolls, so a soft core is the only thing left in the data that reopens the meeting. Waller speaks four and a half hours ahead of it at 09:00Z; Bailey speaks tonight at 17:25Z and the BoJ Summary of Opinions lands at 23:50Z. Then the December cluster: RBA December 8, FOMC and Bank of Canada and RBNZ December 9, SNB December 10, ECB and BoE December 17, BoJ December 18.

dailyRead: The thing that changed over the weekend is not a number, it is a conditional. Trump told CNN on Sunday that restarting the war on Iran is highly unlikely if talks progress, that it depends on whether or not they sign a very strong agreement, and that the carriers remain locked and loaded, while posting that Task Force Iron Gate is in full force and effect. That is not peace and it must not be traded as peace. But it is the first time the administration has tied its restraint to a negotiation rather than to an election date, and it lands on a board where six of these eight central banks built their hawkish case on an energy input. Read what the barrel did, because it is more eloquent than the headlines. The IRGC said on Sunday it had hit three more tankers in an unauthorised channel, Iran's navy said another struck a mine east of the Strait, UK maritime authorities confirmed two incidents, the UAE pulled 22 crew out of the water, Washington widened its blockade of Iranian ports and disabled a commercial vessel in the Gulf of Oman, and Tehran lifted its missile limits. Into all of that, oil fell again: TradingEconomics has WTI at 90.175 and minus 0.72% with Brent at 97.088 and minus 1.25%, after the steepest weekly collapse since the 2020 pandemic - Brent about minus 17% and WTI minus 13% across the November 2 to 6 calendar week on the wire count, minus 7.33% and minus 6.52% on TradingEconomics' own rolling window. Monday's reporting attributes the latest leg to recovering Middle Eastern supply, the prospect of oversupply and a reported Iraqi agreement on Hormuz exports, and that last item is not independently confirmed. So the market is pricing a diplomatic resolution while the physical war intensifies, and the split that creates is the whole trade. The Fed's case is domestic and survives it: October payrolls plus 165,000 against forecasts near plus 60,000, unemployment 4.1%, Q3 growth 3.4%, core 2.6%, and December now priced at roughly 78% to 80% on CME FedWatch against 76.8% on November 6 and about 70% before the payrolls. Tuesday's CPI covers October and therefore predates all of this, and November's lands December 10, the day after the vote. Every other hawkish case here is imported, and every one of them is deflating. Bailey made a further hike explicitly conditional on no progress toward resolving the conflict, and progress is precisely what was announced on Sunday, so his own trigger is disarming rather than arming - with Pill having already said on November 6 that nothing is baked in and that Bank Rate could even fall if growth stalls. Macklem defended the October Canadian hike by pointing at the Middle East energy impulse, and that impulse has lost about a sixth of its value into a labour market that has now contracted two months running with unemployment at a six-month-high 6.7%. The RBA named fuel first among the three reasons for its November 3 hike to 4.85%. The RBNZ's 4.4% December inflation forecast is largely fuel pass-through. And the ECB's 4.0% October headline was delivered by energy at 20.8% with core stuck at 2.5%, while euro-area gas has fallen another 8.68% on the week to 86.62 and German gas 17.40% to 87.04. The position that quietly broke is the franc. It won last week outright as the only currency to gain against the dollar, on pure haven flow with the SNB at zero, and its October CPI of 1.5% is roughly 96% energy against core at 0.5% - so there was never a policy leg, only a war leg, and the war leg is what Sunday removed. That is why CHF's forward turns from balanced to easing today even though the backward verdict stays positive and USD/CHF is still only minus 0.10% at 0.81954: the price has not moved but the reason for holding it has, and EUR/CHF at 0.9148 now has a December ECB hike, a vanishing haven bid and the SNB's own intervention threshold all pointing the same way. The cleanest consequence is that yesterday's named invalidation for the Canadian short - a sustained WTI move back above roughly 95 dollars - has receded rather than triggered, so USD/CAD goes up in conviction rather than down at 1.41035. Elsewhere Monday is a modest risk-on bounce and not a turn. The Kiwi leads at plus 0.95% to 0.55988 on the election, which Westpac itself called a muted response with the uncertainty discount only partially unwound and the larger reaction waiting for the official result on November 27. The Aussie is plus 0.37% to 0.68893 with copper plus 1.53% to 6.3133, both inside a week that was minus 1.57% and a copper month that is minus 5.75%, so neither has earned an upgrade. Gold is back above 4,100 at 4119.43 and plus 1.20%, silver near 53 at 52.831 and plus 1.83%, and the reason given in the wires is that lower oil eases inflation pressure rather than that havens are bid - which is the tell that this is a real-rates trade and not a war trade, and it is capped by the same 80% December odds that are keeping the dollar index subdued at 102.090 and minus 0.20%. Equities are the one unambiguously weak leg, the DAX minus 1.92% at 25,734.60 and the Euro Stoxx 50 minus 0.98% at 6,162.50 on the AI and technology rout, with Euro Stoxx Banks minus 1.11% but still plus 23.06% on the year. The week's order of business is narrow: Bailey at 17:25Z tonight into the BoJ Summary of Opinions at 23:50Z, then US CPI at 13:30Z on Tuesday with Waller four and a half hours ahead of it and the Bank of Canada deliberations that evening, UK GDP on Thursday morning and Lagarde on Thursday night.

today.read: The bounce is the dovish political tail coming off rather than a change in the rate case: the incumbent bloc holds 67 of 131 seats against a 66-seat threshold, so Labour's pledge to restore the Reserve Bank's dual mandate is off the table for this term. USD.when: December 9, with new Economic Projections and no November meeting
USD.note: Held at a 3.75%-4.00% target range on October 28 with two policymakers voting for a hike; TradingEconomics carries 4.00% for October as the upper bound. CME FedWatch has firmed again to roughly 78% to 80% for December, from 76.8% on November 6 and about 70% before the payrolls. The October labour print was hawkish on every line: payrolls plus 165,000 against forecasts near plus 60,000 to 65,000, August revised to 186,000 and September to 60,000, unemployment 4.1% against a 4.2% forecast, average hourly earnings plus 0.4% m/m. This is the one case on the board that de-escalation does not touch, and the reason is calendar as much as composition: Tuesday's CPI is October's and predates the energy collapse, November's lands December 10, the day after the vote, and the domestic case stands on its own at headline 3.7%, core 2.6% and Q3 growth 3.4%. Two things keep it short of certainty. The first is that the price action has stopped paying for the odds - the dollar index is 102.090 and minus 0.20% with 80% priced, and the wires attribute that to lower oil easing inflation pressure, so the marginal buyer has gone. The second is the Michigan preliminary easing year-ahead inflation expectations to 4.3% from 4.7% and long-run to 3.4% from 3.5%, with TradingEconomics wage growth slowing to 4.13% from 4.22%. Waller speaks Tuesday at 09:00Z, four and a half hours before the print; Bowman, Goolsbee and Barkin speak today.

EUR.when: December 17, the final 2026 meeting, with the input behind the case still deflating
EUR.note: Deposit facility 2.50% and the main refinancing rate 2.65%, both TradingEconomics-verified today, held on October 29 after a discussion of a hike that ended in a unanimous hold. The hawkish chorus has grown rather than shrunk: Zigman said on November 5 there is a rather big chance rates will be raised in December, Nagel calls a hike very likely to be necessary, Panetta says it may be needed, ING's Brzeski reads the inflation data as bringing the Bank one step closer and UOB expects a December hike followed by a pause, while Lagarde has signalled the possibility without committing. What has not improved is the quality of the evidence underneath. The October flash HICP of 4.0% was delivered by energy at 20.8% with core at 2.5%, monthly momentum plus 0.4%, headline wage growth down to 3.0% from 3.4% and negotiated wages 2.44% from 2.56%; growth is cooling at 0.4% q/q from 0.6% and 1.3% y/y. And the energy term keeps falling - euro-area gas 86.62 and minus 8.68% on the week, German gas 87.04 and minus 17.40%. Pricing has not resolved, it has widened: available sources span roughly 60% to about 90% for December 17 and cannot be reconciled from what is public, so it should not be quoted as a single number. Eurostat finalises October on November 18. Nagel speaks Wednesday at 08:20Z, the Economic Bulletin and the EU Commission forecasts land Thursday, and Lagarde speaks Thursday at 19:30Z before departing early on February 7, 2027.

GBP.when: December 17, with February 2027 the next realistic move
GBP.note: Bank Rate was raised 25bp to 4.00% on November 5 on an 8-1 vote, with Catherine Mann preferring 0.5 points to 4.25%, so all nine members wanted a hike; TradingEconomics carries 4.00% for November against 3.75% previously. The Monetary Policy Report projects CPI rising to around 5% by the middle of next year from 3.5% now, then falling as energy effects fade. The decisive development is that Bailey wrote his own conditional and Sunday disarmed it. His formulation was that a further increase may be warranted unless there is progress towards resolving the conflict - and progress is exactly what Trump announced, with UK gas at 215.52 and minus 8.25% on the week on top of last week's collapse. Chief economist Huw Pill had already said on November 6 that nothing is baked in for next year, that Bank Rate could stay on hold or even fall if growth stalls, that he is sceptical of the further hikes the market curve carries and that decisive evidence will not arrive until spring 2027; Bailey had called the curve above 4.00% largely risk premia rather than expected rates, direct pushback on the 4.25% February median in the Bank's own Market Participants Survey, and Alan Taylor's framing in the minutes is that this is not the start of a hiking cycle. The remaining hawkish anchor is domestic rather than imported, and it is real: CPI 3.5% with core 2.8% and both rising, unemployment down to 4.7% from 4.9% and employment plus 102,000. Bailey speaks tonight at 17:25Z, Breeden, Lombardelli and Pill all speak Tuesday, and Thursday's GDP m/m is forecast at 0.0% against plus 0.1% with prelim Q3 at plus 0.7%.

JPY.when: December 18, nine days after the Fed, with the Summary of Opinions tonight
JPY.note: Held at 1.25% on October 30 in an 8-1 vote, Takata dissenting for a faster move toward neutral, after consecutive hikes in June and September took the rate to its highest since April 1995; TradingEconomics carries 1.25% for October. The October statement remains the hawkish anchor: the Bank said underlying CPI inflation had aligned with the 2% target for the first time since the target was set in 2013, that financial conditions remain accommodative and that persistent labour shortages sustain a moderate wage-price cycle, while the quarterly outlook lifted the FY2027 inflation forecast to 2.6% from 2.4% and Ueda said the policy phase is changing. The split in the evidence is wide and has not closed: market pricing sits around 68.4% while more than 80% of economists surveyed expect a move to 1.50%, and Ueda's scheduled Friday appearance was the test that tested nothing - his IMF Camdessus lecture on Japan's current account surplus contains no reference to the policy rate, monetary policy, December, the 2% target or the exchange rate. Tonight's Summary of Opinions at 23:50Z is the next real read on how close the board is. The structural weights are unchanged: Takaichi's fiscal expansion, and a haven that is not functioning as one - the yen is only plus 0.15% at 158.227 on a day when gold rose 1.20%. Underlying inflation 2.1%, core also 2.1%, September wage growth accelerating to 4.6% from 3.9%. The Fed voting on December 9 and the Bank on December 18 is the sequencing risk, because a Fed-only hike widens the gap toward the 160 line against which Japan has spent a record 27 trillion yen this year; the three-month high is 160.24.

AUD.when: December 8, with the minutes on November 17
AUD.note: Hiked 25bp to 4.85% on November 3 on a 6-3 majority with three members preferring a hold - the fifth increase this year and the highest cash rate since late 2008 - TradingEconomics-verified for November. The statement named three reasons: elevated fuel and commodity prices amid the Middle East conflict, tighter domestic capacity constraints, and AI-related demand for technology goods. Sunday damaged the first one further and the second is where the argument now sits. Fuel is the reason the Bank put first, and it has fallen about a sixth since the decision with the political path now pointing the same way. AI-related demand is what copper spent last week pricing out, and today's plus 1.53% to 6.3133 sits inside a month that is minus 5.75% and a week that was minus 3.52%; the physical counter-signal is weaker than it looks, because SMM states the record Shanghai and Yangshan premiums are not accompanied by stronger end-use demand and the heavy backwardation runs into a November 16 expiry, which makes it a near-dated delivery squeeze rather than wiring demand. Domestic capacity cannot be checked until the November 17 minutes, and that is now the only live hawkish test. The hawkish residue is narrow but genuine: Q3 CPI 4.3% with core 3.6% and quarterly inflation accelerating to 1.3% q/q from 0.6%, and the Bank expecting inflation above 3% for the coming year. Against it, its own forecasts have growth slowing, housing prices falling significantly and unemployment rising more than previously anticipated, September employment fell 39,300, growth has slowed to 2.1% y/y from 2.5% and Bullock offered no forward guidance. December reads as a pause and February is the meeting being traded.

NZD.when: December 9 with a full Monetary Policy Statement, under a one-seat government
NZD.note: The October 28 hold at 2.75% defied market expectations for a 25bp hike and split 4-3, with members agreeing further tightening would likely be needed depending on the outlook; TradingEconomics carries 2.75% for October. That guidance is the only reason this still reads as a hike and the conviction behind it is low, because the Bank flagged uncertainty over near-term inflation from volatile oil and fuel prices and its hawkish case runs through a 4.4% December inflation forecast that is largely fuel pass-through - into a fuel complex that has now lost about a sixth of its value with the political path pointing the same way. The domestic data sits at the dovish end and has not improved: Q3 unemployment 5.7% and the highest since 2016, private wage growth 2.0% against 3.7% headline inflation, employment minus 0.1% on the quarter, growth 0.2% q/q, and the Bank's own note that wage growth remains subdued with medium-term expectations stable. The forecaster distribution a month out is unusually wide: Citi has scrapped its hike forecasts and expects the OCR on hold through 2027, Commerzbank still expects hikes in December and Q1 2027, and ANZ expects 25bp at each of the next three meetings. The political question has half-resolved and the market has told us how much that is worth. The incumbent National-ACT-NZ First bloc holds 67 of 131 seats against a 66-seat threshold inflated by eleven overhang seats, so Labour's pledge to restore the Reserve Bank's dual mandate is off the table for this term - but the Kiwi gained only about 0.5% to 0.95% on the first session, Westpac called the response muted and said the uncertainty discount can only be partially unwound now, and it expects the larger reaction when the official result is declared on November 27. The Financial Stability Report lands November 10.

CAD.when: December 9, with the energy rationale for the last hike now gone rather than merely weakened
CAD.note: Hiked 25bp to 2.50% on October 28, TradingEconomics-verified for October against 2.25% previously, and Macklem defended it on November 3 by pointing at the energy impulse from the Middle East conflict. That rationale has now been removed twice over: the barrel has lost about a sixth of its value since the decision, and Sunday attached the administration's restraint to a negotiation, which is what kept the complex falling through three more tanker strikes. The domestic data has gone the other way the whole time. The October labour force survey fell 4,700 for a second consecutive decline, full-time employment fell 18,100, unemployment rose to a six-month-high 6.7% from 6.5% and the employment rate slipped to 60.5%; inflation is 3.1% with core at 2.2% and growth 1.1% y/y, so there is no domestic case to replace the imported one. That combination - a bank that tightened on an input which immediately deflated, into a labour market posting consecutive contractions - is why Canada remains the cleanest short against the dollar on this board. The important change today is that yesterday's named invalidation has receded rather than triggered: the risk was a sustained WTI move back above roughly 95 dollars reversing the energy leg, and the political path now points away from it, which is why conviction goes up rather than down. Tuesday's Summary of Deliberations at 18:30Z is the live test of how much of the October hike rested on crude, and Canada is closed Wednesday.

CHF.when: December 10, at zero and with intervention the only active instrument
CHF.note: The SNB policy rate is 0.00%, TradingEconomics-verified for October, held at the September 24 meeting, and there is no case on this data for moving it in either direction on December 10. That is precisely the problem with being long the franc now, and it is today's thesis change. The franc's strength has always been a flow story rather than a policy story - it won last week outright as the only currency to gain against the dollar, taking EUR/CHF to about 0.9148 - and the flow was a war bid. Sunday attached American restraint to a negotiation, which is the single thing that takes that bid away. The inflation line that looks like a case is not one: October CPI printed 1.5% from 1.0% but it was roughly 96% energy with core at 0.5%, and the energy input has fallen another 8.68% in euro-area gas and 17.40% in German gas on the week, so the next print mechanically unwinds much of it. Wage growth has slowed to 0.4% from 1.8%. Growth is the one genuinely strong line at 2.3% y/y and 1.5% q/q, with unemployment stable at 3.0%. What matters for the path is the Bank's stated readiness to intervene in FX, and that risk points the same way as the fundamentals now - against the franc, not for it, with Commerzbank reading 0.9148 as close to where the Bank has previously threatened stronger action. The franc is therefore the one position on this board where the backward verdict and the forward lean genuinely disagree, and a Hormuz re-escalation is what would prove the forward lean wrong.

geopolitics: The transmission chain reversed again over the weekend, and this time it reversed on words rather than on barrels. Trump told CNN on Sunday that restarting the war on Iran is highly unlikely if talks on the nuclear programme and the reopening of the Strait progress, that it depends on whether or not they sign a very strong agreement, and that he retains the option to strike - while posting that Task Force Iron Gate is in full force and effect and commentators noted no sign of a large-scale operation. Rubio had said on October 31 that no choice has been made. Qatar continues to mediate and has denied reports that the two sides failed to reach a deal. That is a conditional and not a settlement, and it must not be traded as one. What makes it the most important fact on this board is what it was strong enough to override. The physical war intensified through the same weekend: the IRGC said on November 8 that three non-compliant tankers exploded and caught fire in an unauthorised channel, Iran's navy said separately that a tanker caught fire after striking a naval mine east of the Strait, UK maritime authorities confirmed incidents involving two tankers with no crew casualties, the UAE rescued 22 crew in the Gulf of Oman, the US military said it had disabled a commercial vessel there, Washington widened its naval blockade of Iranian ports, and Tehran lifted its missile limits. Reuters could not independently confirm the Iranian claims, and Iranian state television said officials had not confirmed reported missile strikes on Qeshm Island. The Strait remains effectively closed with traffic well below pre-war levels. Into all of that, the barrel fell: TradingEconomics has WTI at 90.175 and minus 0.72% with Brent at 97.088 and minus 1.25%, after a calendar week the wires put at Brent minus 17% and WTI minus 13%, the steepest since the 2020 pandemic, and Monday's reporting attributes the continuation to recovering Middle Eastern supply, the prospect of oversupply and a reported Iraqi agreement on Hormuz exports that is not independently confirmed and should not be relied on. The gas complex tells the same story and is the cleaner signal because it is European: euro-area gas 86.62 and minus 8.68% on the week, German gas 87.04 and minus 5.53% on the day and minus 17.40% on the week, UK gas 215.52 and minus 8.25%. The FX read follows from one observation: a market that keeps selling energy through three tanker strikes and a widened blockade has stopped pricing the war and started pricing the negotiation. First, that makes the Canadian dollar the cleanest short on the board again rather than the most dangerous one - yesterday's named invalidation was a sustained WTI move above roughly 95 and Sunday pushed the barrel the other way, so USD/CAD goes up in conviction to high. Second, it breaks the franc, which is today's real change: the franc won last week outright as the only currency to gain against the dollar, and that was a war bid with no policy leg behind it, because the SNB is at zero and the Swiss 1.5% headline is roughly 96% energy against core at 0.5%. CHF/JPY is both the cleanest expression of that and the live test, because an escalation that finally bids the yen is exactly what would prove it wrong. Third, every central bank that built a hawkish case on this input is now exposed to a political timetable rather than a data one - the Bank of England most explicitly, because Bailey wrote the conditional himself and progress is what was announced; then the Bank of Canada, where Macklem named the energy impulse; then the RBA, which named fuel first of three reasons; then the RBNZ, whose 4.4% December forecast is largely fuel pass-through; then the ECB, whose 4.0% headline is energy at 20.8%. Fourth, the dollar is the only case that needs neither outcome, because it is domestic and because the Fed votes on December 9 without ever seeing this in a CPI print. Fifth, the honest expression of the oil view is a short with the reversal named rather than a conviction trade: the complex has whipsawed repeatedly, WTI is still plus 57.04% on the year, and the physical market has not loosened - only the expectation has.
